title: Valley-Selective Transport through Structural Domain Walls in Rhombohedral Graphene Quarter Metals
authors: Vo Tien Phong, Pablo San-Jose, Bing Cheng, Zhengguang Lu, Elsa Prada, Long Ju, Eugene Mele, Cyprian Lewandowski, Francisco Guinea
abstract: Domain walls separating quarter metals with opposite valley polarizations have recently been imaged in rhombohedral graphene multilayers. Depending on their formation mechanism, these walls respond in distinct ways to external magnetic probes. Therefore, understanding their behaviors is critical to the interpretation of experimental results. In this work, we examine domain walls formed from strain-induced one-dimensional structural defects that separate domains with complementary rhombohedral stacking orders. We show that while transport across such domain walls is controlled by the valley degree of freedom, the coupling to a magnetic field is dictated by the momentum-space chirality encoded in the Hamiltonian. As a consequence, structural domain walls are rendered electronically opaque by an applied magnetic field, while intrinsic domain walls formed by spontaneous valley symmetry breaking are unstable in the presence of such an ordering field and can be eliminated. This dichotomy allows the two types of domain walls to be distinguished in a magnetotransport experiment.
summary: This work investigates domain walls in graphene quarter metals, differentiating between structural defects and intrinsic symmetry-broken walls. By analyzing their electronic transport properties, the authors show that structural walls are magnetically opaque, while intrinsic walls are unstable in a magnetic field. This dichotomy offers a robust method for experimental characterization of these exotic quantum states.
main_problem: The study aims to distinguish between two types of domain walls (structural vs. intrinsic) in rhombohedral graphene quarter metals by analyzing their distinct responses to external magnetic fields.
main_result: Structural domain walls are rendered electronically opaque by an applied magnetic field, whereas intrinsic domain walls are unstable and can be eliminated by such a field, allowing for experimental differentiation.
method: The analysis employs continuum models and tight-binding calculations to determine the transmission properties across the domain walls based on valley and chirality degrees of freedom.
model_or_system: The system is rhombohedral graphene multilayers hosting quarter metals, modeled using continuum Hamiltonians and tight-binding approaches that incorporate valley polarization and structural defects.
key_observables: Transmission ($T$) as a function of energy and momentum, and the electronic opacity/stability of the domain walls.

main_assumptions: The analysis relies on continuum models assuming sharp walls and specific relationships between valley and chirality for structural defects.
figures_summary: Figures show SNOM imaging of structural domain walls, schematics of walls induced by strain, and plots of transmission vs. energy/momentum for both continuum and tight-binding models.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical context of domain walls, then develops theoretical models (continuum/tight-binding) to calculate transport, culminating in the key result distinguishing the two wall types based on magnetic field response.
why_interesting:
The clear distinction between transport control by valley ($\xi$) versus magnetic coupling by chirality ($
u$) provides a powerful, measurable signature for probing topological or symmetry-protected states in condensed matter systems.
